note.7-10: Jesus says you are a light. Lights are for showing other people the way.
note.11-14: A light is not for looking at — it is for seeing by. Your life is meant to help other people see God.
note.15-18: The metaphor is public by design. Jesus assumes discipleship is visible, and that visibility points away from the disciple and towards the Father.

note.7-10: A shepherd looks after the sheep all day and all night. God looks after you like that.
note.11-14: David had been a shepherd himself. He knew exactly how much work it takes to keep sheep safe — and he says God does that for him.
note.15-18: Written by a shepherd about being shepherded. The psalm's turn from 'he' to 'you' in verse four happens exactly where the valley does.

note.7-10: God loves the world so much that he gave his own Son. That includes you.
note.11-14: The most famous verse in the Bible is not mainly about us believing. It is about God giving.
note.15-18: Note what verse 17 rules out: the sending is not for condemnation. Judgement is real in John's gospel, but it is not the purpose of the incarnation.

note.7-10: God says: do not be afraid, I am with you. He is holding your hand.
note.11-14: 'Do not fear' is not the same as 'nothing frightening will happen'. The reason given is a person, not a promise about circumstances.
note.15-18: The grounds for the imperative are covenantal — 'I am your God' — not circumstantial. Fear is answered by presence, not by explanation.

note.7-10: Paul says he can do things because Jesus gives him strength.
note.11-14: Paul writes this from prison, about having plenty and having nothing. It is about endurance, not winning.
note.15-18: Context matters: verses 11–12 define 'all things' as contentment in abundance and in need. It is a verse about sufficiency, not achievement.

note.7-10: Jesus gives one new rule: love each other the way he loved you.
note.11-14: Jesus says the world will recognise his followers by one thing — how they treat each other.
note.15-18: 'As I have loved you' sets the measure impossibly high and is spoken hours before the cross, which is where the measure gets defined.

note.7-10: Trust God more than you trust your own ideas.
note.11-14: 'Lean not on your own understanding' does not mean stop thinking. It means stop making your own understanding the final word.
note.15-18: The wisdom tradition prizes understanding — which makes this instruction pointed. Even good reasoning is a servant, not a master.

note.7-10: Jesus says he is the good shepherd who gives his life for the sheep.
note.11-14: A hired man runs when a wolf comes. Jesus contrasts himself with everyone whose care has a limit.
note.15-18: The claim is deliberately provocative against Ezekiel 34's indictment of Israel's shepherds. Jesus is answering a prophetic charge.

note.7-10: God tells Joshua to be brave, because God will be with him everywhere.
note.11-14: Joshua is taking over from Moses — an impossible act to follow. The command to be brave comes with a reason attached.
note.15-18: The threefold repetition through the chapter is a commissioning formula. Courage is commanded, which implies it is not merely a temperament.

note.7-10: If you are tired, Jesus says: come to me and rest.
note.11-14: A yoke is what oxen wear to pull a load. Jesus does not offer no yoke — he offers a better one.
note.15-18: The 'rest' language deliberately echoes the sabbath and the promised land. Jesus places himself where those institutions stood.

note.7-10: God made you on purpose, and he knows everything about you.
note.11-14: David says God knew him before anyone else could. Being fully known and still loved is the point.
note.15-18: The psalm's anthropology is uncompromising: personhood begins with God's knowledge and craft, not with anyone's recognition.

note.7-10: Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness — these grow in you like fruit on a tree.
note.11-14: Fruit is grown, not manufactured. Paul lists character, not achievements.
note.15-18: Singular 'fruit', plural qualities — the grammar resists treating these as a menu to pick from.

note.7-10: Jesus says to keep asking God, like a child asking a good dad.
note.11-14: The argument is from lesser to greater: if flawed parents give good things, how much more God.
note.15-18: The 'how much more' structure is rabbinic. The point is not that prayer is a vending machine but that God's character is not stingy.

title: A friend loves at all times

note.7-10: A real friend is still your friend when things go wrong.
note.11-14: The proverb defines friendship by what survives trouble, not by what happens on a good day.
note.15-18: Hebrew wisdom repeatedly tests relationships against adversity — the standard is durability, not intensity.

note.7-10: Instead of worrying, tell God what you need — and say thank you.
note.11-14: Paul does not say 'don't feel anxious'. He says do something specific with the anxiety.
note.15-18: The peace promised 'guards' — a garrison metaphor — and is explicitly said to exceed comprehension rather than resolve the problem.

note.7-10: Love God with everything you are, and love other people like you love yourself.
note.11-14: A scribe asks Jesus to rank 613 commandments. Jesus answers with two, and refuses to separate them.
note.15-18: Jesus binds Deuteronomy 6:5 to Leviticus 19:18 — a move that is not original to him, but the weight he gives it is.

note.7-10: Nothing at all can stop God loving you. Nothing.
note.11-14: Paul makes a list of everything he can think of that might separate us from God, then rules all of it out.
note.15-18: The list is cosmological — powers, height, depth — because Paul is answering the ancient fear that fate or the powers outrank God's love.

note.7-10: God calls you his child. That is what you are.
note.11-14: John is amazed by the word 'children' — not servants, not followers. Family.
note.15-18: The aorist 'has given' plus present 'we are' sets adoption as a completed act with a continuing status.

note.7-10: God's word is like a lamp that shows you where to put your feet.
note.11-14: An oil lamp lit one step ahead, not the whole road. That is the kind of light being promised.
note.15-18: The image is modest on purpose: guidance in Scripture is sufficient for the next step rather than exhaustive about the route.

note.7-10: Following Jesus means putting him first, even when it is hard.
note.11-14: 'Daily' is the word that makes this ordinary. Most cross-carrying is unremarkable.
note.15-18: Luke's addition of 'daily' domesticates nothing — it extends martyrdom's logic into the whole of an ordinary life.

note.7-10: We can love because God loved us first.
note.11-14: Our love is a response, not the thing that starts the relationship.
note.15-18: The priority of divine love is the structural point of the letter and rules out love as a qualification for being loved.

note.7-10: Give God the things that worry you. He cares about you.
note.11-14: 'He cares for you' is the reason given — not 'because worry is useless'.
note.15-18: The participle ties casting anxiety to the humility of verse 6: refusing to carry it yourself is an act of submission, not of denial.

note.7-10: Even young people get tired. God gives new strength to those who wait for him.
note.11-14: The promise is not that you will not get tired. It is that strength is renewed, again and again.
note.15-18: The chapter's argument runs from God's incomparability to the exhaustion of the strongest — waiting is what creatures do.

note.7-10: Salt makes food taste good. Jesus says you make a difference like that.
note.11-14: Salt in the ancient world preserved food from going bad. It was not decoration.
note.15-18: The warning about salt losing saltiness is aimed at a discipleship that becomes indistinguishable from its surroundings.

note.7-10: God made everything. He started with light.
note.11-14: The first thing said about God is that he makes. Everything that exists is on purpose.
note.15-18: The text's polemic edge shows against its neighbours' myths: no conflict, no rival gods, and the sun and moon demoted to lamps.

note.7-10: The boy came home, and his dad ran to meet him.
note.11-14: In that culture a grown man did not run. The father humiliates himself to reach his son first.
note.15-18: The parable is the third of three, and the elder brother is the one the audience is meant to identify with.

note.7-10: Faith is being sure about things you cannot see yet.
note.11-14: The chapter that follows defines faith by what people did, not by what they felt.
note.15-18: 'Hypostasis' — substance, assurance — is stronger than 'hope'. Faith is treated as evidential, not merely psychological.

note.7-10: Anyone who belongs to Jesus is made new.
note.11-14: 'The old has gone' is written to a church that was still a mess. New does not mean finished.
note.15-18: The phrase is arguably 'there is a new creation' — a cosmological claim, not only a personal one.

note.7-10: Jesus says happy are the gentle, the kind, and the peacemakers.
note.11-14: Every group Jesus calls blessed is a group the world tends to overlook.
note.15-18: The beatitudes describe the citizens of the kingdom rather than prescribe entry requirements — indicative before imperative.

note.7-10: God wants you to be fair, be kind, and walk close to him.
note.11-14: Micah answers a question about sacrifices with a demand about how you live.
note.15-18: The verse is the prophetic summary of covenant obligation, set against a religion that had become transactional.

note.7-10: Do everything as if you were doing it for Jesus — even homework.
note.11-14: This was first written to slaves. Paul dignifies work nobody else thought worth dignifying.
note.15-18: The household code's radicalism lies in addressing subordinate members as moral agents at all — unusual in its genre.

note.7-10: Good friends make each other better, like two knives being sharpened.
note.11-14: Sharpening makes sparks. Friendships that improve you are not always comfortable.
note.15-18: The proverb assumes friction as constitutive of formation rather than as a failure of friendship.

note.7-10: When your heart is broken, God comes close.
note.11-14: God is not described as near to the strong. He is near to the crushed.
note.15-18: The psalm pairs divine nearness with contrition rather than merit, which is why it recurs in pastoral use.

note.7-10: Jesus told his friends to tell everyone about him — and that he would always be with them.
note.11-14: The commission ends with a promise: 'I am with you always'. The task comes with company.
note.15-18: The authority claim in verse 18 grounds the imperative; Matthew closes with Immanuel, as he opened.

note.7-10: When you know you are loved, you do not need to be scared.
note.11-14: The fear John means is fear of punishment — the fear of not being acceptable.
note.15-18: The logic is forensic: assurance at judgement is the specific fear love resolves, not anxiety in general.

note.7-10: God feeds the birds. He will look after you too.
note.11-14: Jesus does not argue that worry is wrong. He argues that it does not work.
note.15-18: The argument moves from lesser to greater within a creation theology — providence, not optimism.

note.7-10: Be kind and patient with people, and forgive them.
note.11-14: 'Bear with each other' assumes the other person will be annoying. It is realistic, not sentimental.
note.15-18: The virtue list is clothing imagery — deliberate, daily, and put on rather than felt.

note.7-10: This is a very old prayer that God gave for blessing people.
note.11-14: Priests said these words over Israel for centuries. They are still said over people today.
note.15-18: The oldest known copy of any biblical text is a silver amulet carrying this blessing — a striking material continuity.

note.7-10: Put God first, and he will take care of the rest.
note.11-14: 'First' is about order, not about doing more religious things.
note.15-18: The verse closes an argument about anxiety; the kingdom is offered as the alternative organising principle to security-seeking.

note.7-10: Be glad, keep praying, and say thank you.
note.11-14: Three short commands, written to a church under pressure. 'In all circumstances' is not 'for all circumstances'.
note.15-18: The prepositions matter: thanksgiving in every circumstance is commanded; thanksgiving for every circumstance is not.

note.7-10: Jesus is God, and he came to live with us.
note.11-14: 'Made his dwelling' literally means pitched his tent — the same word used for God's tent in the desert.
note.15-18: John's prologue deliberately locates the incarnation in Israel's tabernacle theology rather than in Greek metaphysics.

note.7-10: It is better to have someone with you than to be on your own.
note.11-14: Ecclesiastes is a sceptical book. This is one of the things it says is genuinely worth having.
note.15-18: In a book that repeatedly finds effort 'vapour', companionship is one of the few goods the Preacher affirms without irony.

note.7-10: Do not just listen to God's word. Do what it says.
note.11-14: James compares hearing without doing to looking in a mirror and forgetting your own face.
note.15-18: James's polemic targets a religion of assent; the 'law of liberty' language keeps obedience within grace rather than against it.

note.7-10: God has good plans for his people, even when things are hard.
note.11-14: This was written to people in exile who were told to settle down for seventy years. Good plans are not always fast plans.
note.15-18: Reading verse 11 without verses 4–10 turns a national promise, given to a generation who would die in exile, into a personal guarantee.

note.7-10: The shepherd left the ninety-nine to go and find the one who was lost.
note.11-14: The maths is bad and the point is deliberate. One is worth going after.
note.15-18: The parable answers a specific accusation in verse 2 — Jesus is defending his table, not offering a general sentiment.

note.7-10: God waits, because he wants everyone to come to him.
note.11-14: What looks like God being slow is described as God being patient.
note.15-18: Peter reframes eschatological delay as mercy, which is the letter's answer to the scoffers of verse 4.

note.7-10: Give because you want to, not because you have to.
note.11-14: Paul refuses to pressure them, in the middle of asking them for money.
note.15-18: The collection chapters are a case study in Paul's refusal to use apostolic authority for financial leverage.

note.7-10: Jesus is God, but he became a servant for us.
note.11-14: Paul quotes what may be an early hymn. The movement is all downward: God to servant to death.
note.15-18: Whether 'harpagmos' means grasping or exploiting shapes the whole reading; either way the hymn's shape is descent before exaltation.

note.7-10: Be kind and forgive people, because God forgave you.
note.11-14: The measure is not what the other person deserves. It is what you have already received.
note.15-18: Forgiveness here is derivative — 'as God in Christ forgave you' sets both the ground and the pattern.

note.7-10: God is a safe place to run to when you are scared.
note.11-14: The psalm imagines the worst thing the ancient world could picture — the earth giving way — and still says 'we will not fear'.
note.15-18: The refrain structure and the 'be still' of verse 10 are addressed to the nations, not primarily to the anxious individual.

note.7-10: Jesus put a child in the middle and said welcoming a child is welcoming him.
note.11-14: In that world children had no status at all. Jesus puts one in the centre of an argument about greatness.
note.15-18: The saying inverts the honour economy the disciples were arguing inside, and Mark places it immediately after a passion prediction.

note.7-10: Tell the truth, and be kind while you do it.
note.11-14: Truth without love and love without truth are both easier. Paul asks for both at once.
note.15-18: The phrase is participial and communal — it describes how a body grows up into its head, not how to win an argument.

note.7-10: Love is patient and kind. Love never gives up.
note.11-14: Read at weddings, written to a church that was falling out badly. It is a rebuke as much as a poem.
note.15-18: Chapter 13 sits inside an argument about spiritual gifts; its function is to relativise gifting, not to describe romance.
